competitor_matrix.name: Expensify
competitor_matrix.positioning: Mainstream expense-management SaaS built for external, multi-company expense reimbursement, with receipt scanning and configurable multi-step approval workflows layered on top.
competitor_matrix.strengths: A mature, widely-adopted product with strong mobile receipt capture and broad integrations into major accounting systems, so re-keying elsewhere in a company's stack is largely eliminated.
competitor_matrix.weaknesses: Priced and featured for organizations managing external, multi-entity expense management at scale; its feature surface and cost structure are heavier than a single organization's 2-3 step internal approval chain actually needs.
competitor_matrix.reasoning: Directly relevant alternative for the stated approval-chain and re-keying problem; widely known in this category.

competitor_matrix.name: Manual spreadsheet + email tracking (status quo)
competitor_matrix.positioning: The current internal process described in the input: expense claims routed by email through 2-3 sequential manager approvals, tracked ad hoc in spreadsheets rather than any purpose-built system.
competitor_matrix.strengths: Requires no new tooling cost or vendor evaluation, and every employee and approver is already familiar with how it works today.
competitor_matrix.weaknesses: Gives employees no visibility into where their claim is stuck, gives approving managers no dashboard of pending items, and forces Finance Operations staff to manually re-key every claim into the accounting system — the exact pain points named in the problem statement.
competitor_matrix.reasoning: The status quo is itself the most relevant 'competitor' — the input describes it directly.

tam.basis: The external market for the category of software this internal tool would substitute for, e.g. the market Expensify (CM-01) competes in — not a claim about a market this internal tool itself will enter, since it has no external customers.
tam.reasoning: Order-of-magnitude figure from general knowledge of the expense-management SaaS category, not independently verified via a dedicated sizing search; useful only as context for why a commercial alternative like CM-01 is priced the way it is, not as a sizing claim about this project.

sam.value: Not meaningfully estimable — this is a single-organization internal tool with no external customers
sam.basis: SAM ordinarily scopes a serviceable addressable market of customers a product could realistically sell to; an internal-only tool has no such market, so forcing a figure here would be more misleading than informative.
sam.reasoning: Being honest about a genuine dimension mismatch rather than inventing a plausible-sounding figure: this idea is a build-vs-buy decision for one organization's own workflow, not a product being taken to a market, so SAM as conventionally defined does not apply. The closest analogue — the cost this org avoids by not buying CM-01 — is captured under SOM instead.

som.value: Avoided vendor cost only, not independently estimated (illustrative order-of-magnitude: a few thousand USD/year at this org's likely headcount, per CM-01's typical per-seat SaaS pricing)
som.basis: The realistic 'obtainable' value for an internal tool is cost avoidance versus buying CM-01 or an equivalent, scaled to this org's approval-chain headcount as described in target_users, not new revenue captured from a market.
som.reasoning: Low confidence because no actual headcount figure or CM-01 quote was available in the input or search results — this is a directional estimate only, explicitly flagged as such rather than presented as a firm figure.

industry_trends.statement: Growing adoption of digital, mobile-first approval workflows to replace manual/email-based internal approval chains across mid-size organizations.
industry_trends.reasoning: General category trend supporting why a purpose-built internal tool is a reasonable direction rather than continuing the status quo (CM-02); not specific to this org, so kept at moderate rather than high confidence.

customer_insights.insight: Employees submitting claims want real-time visibility into where their claim is stuck in the 2-3 step approval chain, not just eventual notification of approval or rejection.
customer_insights.reasoning: Stated directly in the problem statement ('no visibility into where their claim is stuck') — this is a restatement-with-attribution of an explicit input fact, not an inferred behavior.

customer_insights.insight: Finance Operations staff need claims to arrive in a re-keyable-free format, since manual re-keying into the accounting system is their most time-consuming recurring task.
customer_insights.reasoning: Stated directly in the problem statement ('Finance manually re-keys every claim... consuming hours of staff time each week').

pricing_benchmarks.subject: Expensify
pricing_benchmarks.price_point: Roughly $4-36 per active user per month depending on plan tier (illustrative order-of-magnitude, not independently re-verified against current published pricing)
pricing_benchmarks.reasoning: General knowledge of the per-seat SaaS pricing pattern typical for this competitor category; explicitly flagged as illustrative and not re-verified against Expensify's current published price list, which should be checked before this figure informs a real build-vs-buy decision.

strengths.statement: A purpose-built internal tool can be scoped exactly to this org's 2-3 step approval chain, avoiding the cost and feature overhead of a general-purpose SaaS tool priced and built for external, multi-entity expense management.
strengths.reasoning: Derived from CM-01's weakness (over-featured for this use case) — a narrower internal tool avoids that overhead.

weaknesses.statement: No internal tooling or team experience building approval-workflow software exists yet, so building this in-house starts from zero precedent rather than an established internal platform.
weaknesses.reasoning: Inferred from the problem being currently solved manually (CM-02) — no internal precedent exists to build from.

opportunities.statement: Eliminating Finance's manual re-keying into the accounting system (CI-02) is a clear, measurable efficiency win that the status quo does not offer and that Expensify would only partially deliver given its external-facing scope, aligning with TR-01's broader shift toward digital approval workflows.
opportunities.reasoning: Derived from CI-02 (customer_insights) and CM-02's stated weakness (manual re-keying), reinforced by TR-01's category-level trend.

threats.statement: If Expensify or a similar mainstream tool is already budget-approved elsewhere in the organization, a bespoke internal tool may be perceived as duplicative spend even though it is better scoped to this specific approval chain — and PB-01's per-seat pricing means the org may already be treating that spend as a sunk comparison point.
threats.reasoning: Derived from CM-01 being a mature, already-adopted category of tool in many orgs, combined with PB-01's pricing benchmark.

data_sufficiency.rationale: Competitive intelligence: sufficient — two relevant alternatives reviewed (Expensify and the status quo). Market sizing: thin by nature, not by search failure — this is a single-org internal tool with no external customers, so SAM/SOM as conventionally defined don't meaningfully apply; TAM and SOM are reported as illustrative context/cost-avoidance estimates with capped confidence rather than fabricated firm figures, and SAM is explicitly flagged as not estimable. Industry trends: thin — only one general category trend found, appropriately proportionate to how little a purely internal tool intersects with 'industry' trends. Customer insights: sufficient — both grounded directly in the problem statement's own explicit pain points. Pricing benchmarks: thin — only one illustrative, unverified competitor price point found. Overall judged sufficient for this internal-tool decision because the two dimensions that matter most here (competitive intelligence, customer insights) are well-grounded; market_sizing and pricing_benchmarks are honestly thinner given the nature of an internal-only tool, not padded to look otherwise.

• Key decision: included the manual status-quo process as a 'competitor' since the input describes it as the thing actually being replaced.
